note: Each row is a public record as it was filed or published; the list shows everything the figures in this case were counted from. Being listed is not an accusation: the case file says what is established and what is not.

tables.title: Every registered lobbyist, client by client: contacts made and payments reported
tables.what: One registered lobbyist working for one client at one firm: the contacts with City officials that the lobbyist reported for that client, and the payments from that client entered on the lobbyist’s own monthly reports.

columns.t: Payments from the client on this lobbyist’s reports

sources.t: San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Activity Directory - lobbyists’ monthly reports of contacts, payments from clients, contributions and expenses (DataSF)
San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Directory - registrations (DataSF)

tables.how: Every row of the Ethics Commission’s lobbyist activity file of the kinds “ContactOfPublicOfficial” and “PaymentReceived”, January 2010 to October 2026, grouped by the lobbyist, the firm and the client named on it. The contacts add up to the 66,677 in the case. Two lobbyists at one firm often enter the same client payment on both their reports, so the payment column must not be added up across lobbyists: the next list counts each payment once and is the one that adds up to the case’s total.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown. The figures are what lobbyists filed; nobody audits them against the firms’ books, and a retainer can cover work other than lobbying. A lobbyist typed under two spellings appears twice.

tables.title: What each client paid each lobbying firm, year by year
tables.what: One client’s payments to one lobbying firm (or to its own in-house lobbyists) in one calendar year, as the lobbyists reported them month by month.

sources.t: San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Activity Directory - lobbyists’ monthly reports of contacts, payments from clients, contributions and expenses (DataSF)

tables.how: Every “PaymentReceived” entry in the lobbyist activity file (52,879 entries). Where two lobbyists at one firm report the same client, date and amount it is counted once, as the analysis does; the entries are then added by client, firm and year. The rows add up to the $173,342,300 the case quotes, from 2,520 clients. Rows of zero are left out. The year 2026 runs to October. 338 rows are payments by a private person and name only the firm.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. A company that lobbies with its own employees reports their pay as a payment from itself. Client names are grouped after removing punctuation and company suffixes, which can split one client filed under two names or join two with the same name. The number of payment entries rose far faster than the dollars between 2013 and 2017, which points to fuller reporting of small clients, not a tripling of lobbying.

tables.how: Every “ContactOfPublicOfficial” entry in the lobbyist activity file whose department, as filed, is Board of Supervisors or Mayor’s office (18,392 of the 66,677 contacts in the case; the four lists of contacts together hold all of them). The official is named as the lobbyist typed the name; where the name matches someone with a campaign committee for City office and the contact was at an elected office, the name is shown as the committee register has it. The report link opens the monthly report the entry was filed in.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown. A contact can be a meeting, a call or an e-mail, and one meeting with five officials is five rows. Two people with one name would be merged, and one person typed two ways split. Contact by someone who never registered leaves no row.

tables.how: Every itemized contribution (Schedules A and C) since 2010 to a committee controlled by a City official or candidate, kept when the giver falls in one of five groups: a registered lobbyist (surname and first name match a lobbyist active within a year, and the employer written on the contribution is that lobbyist’s firm or the occupation says lobbyist); another person who gives a firm that sells lobbying as employer; such a firm itself; a client that was paying a lobbyist within a year; or a person who gives such a client as employer with an owner’s, partner’s or senior officer’s title. These are the 2,925 contributions and $1,173,712 in the case. Of the rows counted as a registered lobbyist’s, 635 to City-office committees are dated before the ban of 1 January 2018 and 57 after it. A further 2,699 contributions from people who share a lobbyist’s name but give another employer are not counted and not listed.
tables.limits: Each row is a campaign filing; the employer and occupation are what the giver told the committee. Counting a giver as a registered lobbyist rests on a match of name and employer and is not confirmed: two people can share a name and a workplace. Since 2018 a registered lobbyist may not give to an official the lobbyist is registered to lobby, but a contribution to another office, to a party-committee seat or before the lobbyist registered for that agency is not covered, and the filings do not say which agencies a lobbyist was registered for. Staff of law firms and large companies give for their own reasons. An official can be given to because of what the official already stands for.

San Francisco Board of Supervisors: legislation records with titles, sponsors, dates and outcomes (Legistar; each row links to its file)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: roll-call pages for contracts, grants, leases, appropriations and lobbied measures, 2015 to November 2026 (one page per action; each row links its own page)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: published minutes of 65 Board and committee meetings, 2015 to 2025 (vote lines only; each recovered roll call links its minutes)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: roll-call pages for land-use matters, 2015 to 2026 (Legistar)

tables.how: A contact is tied to a Board file only when the lobbyist’s report gives the six-digit file number and the contact is dated from two years before to three years after the file’s introduction. That gives 294 files, 216 of them passed; 258 are ordinances, resolutions, motions or charter amendments introduced since 2015. The position is read from the “outcome sought” by fixed word lists (support, oppose, amend, monitor or unclear). A file sponsored by “Mayor” is credited to the mayoral candidate lobbyists most often reported contacting at the Mayor’s office around that date. An appeal hearing is shown without its street address.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown. Passing is the normal fate of a Board file, so a lobbied file that passed shows little. Only a small share of contacts carry a usable file number, so most lobbying on legislation is not in this list. A position read from a few typed words can be wrong, and “monitor” often hides one.

tables.title: Every reported contact that cites a Board file by number
tables.what: One reported contact between a lobbyist and an official about a numbered Board file; a contact that cites two files has a row for each.

sources.t: San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Activity Directory - lobbyists’ monthly reports of contacts, payments from clients, contributions and expenses (DataSF)
San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Filings Directory - every registration and monthly report with the date received (DataSF)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: legislation records with titles, sponsors, dates and outcomes (Legistar; each row links to its file)

tables.how: The 2,291 contacts whose report gives a six-digit Board file number that is on record, dated from two years before to three years after the file’s introduction. These are the contacts every test on sponsorship and votes in this case starts from; they also appear in the four lists of all contacts.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown. The file number is what the lobbyist typed. A contact dated after the vote is listed too; the tests that need a contact before the vote say so.

tables.title: Each sitting supervisor on each lobbied Board file: contacted or not, sponsor or not, and the vote
tables.what: One supervisor who was sitting when a lobbied Board file was introduced: whether a lobbyist reported contacting that supervisor about the file, whether the supervisor sponsored it, and the supervisor’s vote on its final roll call.

San Francisco Board of Supervisors: legislation records with titles, sponsors, dates and outcomes (Legistar; each row links to its file)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: roll-call pages for contracts, grants, leases, appropriations and lobbied measures, 2015 to November 2026 (one page per action; each row links its own page)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: published minutes of 65 Board and committee meetings, 2015 to 2025 (vote lines only; each recovered roll call links its minutes)

tables.how: The 258 lobbied ordinances, resolutions, motions and charter amendments introduced since 2015, each set beside every supervisor the roll calls show sitting at its introduction. The rows give the case’s figures: a contacted supervisor was a sponsor in 169 of 629 cases, a supervisor who was not contacted in 398 of 2,277; contacted supervisors cast 522 ayes and 14 noes on final roll calls, 521 of them after a contact dated on or before the day of the vote. A contact counts whenever it falls in the window around the file, including after the vote.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. A lobbyist goes first to the member who wrote the measure, whether to back it or to fight it, so contact follows sponsorship at least as much as the reverse. Most Board files pass without a dissenting vote, so a column of ayes says little about any one member. Whether an aye was what the client wanted is in the lists on votes below.

tables.how: Every final Board roll call on disk where a lobbying client’s side can be read, each file once (307 files, 308 sides, since a file can have clients on both sides): lobbied land-use matters, other measures a lobbyist cited by file number with a contact in the three years up to the vote that sought support or opposed it, and contracts, leases and other money files whose title names as the other party a client then paying a lobbyist. The client’s side carried on 288 of the 308 sides; clients sought defeat on 18 and got it on 1. A client named only in a file’s title has no contacts citing the file, so its lobbyists’ names are in the first list, not here.
tables.limits: Nearly every vote here is an aye on a matter that passed without dissent, so a member who received money and one who did not vote alike; only the divided roll calls can show a difference, and they are few. A lobbyist contacts the members most likely to matter and donors give to members who already agree with them, so even a gap would not show that money moved a vote. The client’s side is read from a few typed words, or from the title of a money file matched to a client by name, and a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote. Members printed as excused or absent are left out: the page does not say whether they stepped aside or were out of the room. The money column adds contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists, their firm and the firm’s staff; the individual contributions are in the list of contributions above. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown.

tables.what: One supervisor’s aye or no on one final Board roll call where a lobbying client’s side can be read, marked as with or against that client, with what the client’s circle had given to that supervisor in the two years before.

tables.how: The 3,297 member votes of the test the case reports: members voted the client’s way in 95.5% of 426 votes where the client’s circle had given to them in the two years before and in 91.5% of 2,871 where it had not. On the 23 divided roll calls the figures are 78.1% of 32 against 75.3% of 215. The analysis then shuffles the giving 4,000 times among the members who voted on the same roll call to see whether the gap is more than chance; it is not.
tables.limits: Nearly every vote here is an aye on a matter that passed without dissent, so a member who received money and one who did not vote alike; only the divided roll calls can show a difference, and they are few. A lobbyist contacts the members most likely to matter and donors give to members who already agree with them, so even a gap would not show that money moved a vote. The client’s side is read from a few typed words, or from the title of a money file matched to a client by name, and a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote. Members printed as excused or absent are left out: the page does not say whether they stepped aside or were out of the room. The money column adds contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists, their firm and the firm’s staff; the individual contributions are in the list of contributions above. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made.

San Francisco Board of Supervisors: roll-call pages for contracts, grants, leases, appropriations and lobbied measures, 2015 to November 2026 (one page per action; each row links its own page)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: published minutes of 65 Board and committee meetings, 2015 to 2025 (vote lines only; each recovered roll call links its minutes)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: roll-call pages for land-use matters, 2015 to 2026 (Legistar)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: legislation records with titles, sponsors, dates and outcomes (Legistar; each row links to its file)
San Francisco Ethics Commission: Campaign Finance - Transactions, all local committees (DataSF)

tables.how: The 46 divided roll calls the case sets out (36 final Board votes, 2 other Board votes on the same measures where a member voted differently, 8 committee votes), every member listed. A file with clients on both sides appears once for each side. On the final votes where a side can be read, members who had money from the client’s circle voted the client’s way 25 of 32 times and the others 162 of 215.
tables.limits: Nearly every vote here is an aye on a matter that passed without dissent, so a member who received money and one who did not vote alike; only the divided roll calls can show a difference, and they are few. A lobbyist contacts the members most likely to matter and donors give to members who already agree with them, so even a gap would not show that money moved a vote. The client’s side is read from a few typed words, or from the title of a money file matched to a client by name, and a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote. Members printed as excused or absent are left out: the page does not say whether they stepped aside or were out of the room. The money column adds contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists, their firm and the firm’s staff; the individual contributions are in the list of contributions above. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. A row here is one vote, not a pattern: supervisors vote in blocs for reasons of politics and district that have nothing to do with a client.

tables.title: Lobbied measures whose clients sought passage: each sitting supervisor, sponsor or not, and the circle’s giving
tables.what: One supervisor sitting when a lobbied measure was introduced: whether that supervisor sponsored it, and what the circle of the clients who sought its passage had given to that supervisor’s committees in the two years before.

columns.t: From those clients’ circle to this supervisor’s committees, two years before introduction

sources.t: San Francisco Ethics Commission: Lobbyist Activity Directory - lobbyists’ monthly reports of contacts, payments from clients, contributions and expenses (DataSF)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: legislation records with titles, sponsors, dates and outcomes (Legistar; each row links to its file)
San Francisco Ethics Commission: Campaign Finance - Transactions, all local committees (DataSF)
San Francisco Board of Supervisors: enacted ordinances 2018 to 2026 with sponsors and titles, as indexed from Legistar (each row links to its file)

tables.how: The 97 ordinances, resolutions, motions and charter amendments introduced since 2015 that a client lobbied in support of and that a sitting supervisor sponsored, each beside every supervisor then sitting (1,088 cases). A supervisor was a sponsor in 46 of 111 cases where the circle had given and in 293 of 977 where it had not. Shuffling the giving among the supervisors sitting for each measure gives 41.4 on average against 46 observed, which is within chance.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a row is a report the lobbyist filed, not a finding about anyone. Sponsors and donors find each other because they agree: a business group gives to the supervisors who share its outlook and those supervisors write the measures it likes. A gap would show association, not cause. Measures tied to lobbying by the words of the subject are an inference and are marked.

tables.what: One passed Board file about a contract, lease, grant, settlement or other money matter, and one client named in its title that was paying a lobbyist around that time.

tables.how: The Board’s passed money files introduced since 2011, with the other party read from each title and matched by name to a lobbying client active within two years of introduction; gifts and grants the City receives are left out. 136 files, 49 of them with a named sponsor. A final Board roll call is on disk for 126: 117 with no vote against and 9 divided. The amount is the figure in the title; where a title names several parties and several amounts, only a figure in the same clause as this party.
tables.limits: The other party is read from the title and matched to a client by name, which can join two different firms. Such a client has usually won a department’s competition before the Board votes, and the amount is not always money to the client: under a lease or sale of City property, a cost-sharing agreement or a settlement the client may be the one paying. The same amount is repeated on each row of a file that names two clients, so the column total counts it twice.

tables.how: For each money file in the list above that has a sponsor, and for the 38 files that are gifts or grants a lobbying client made to the City (listed, not counted): the client’s payments to its lobbyists, contacts by its lobbyists with the sponsor in the three years before passage, and contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists and their firms to the sponsor’s committees. A pair is listed when there was a contact or a contribution. The client’s lobbyists had contacted the sponsor on 13 files, its circle had given on 8, and both on 2; all four links are present in 1 pair. 2 budget add-backs naming a lobbying client are added from the add-back lists.
tables.limits: Most contracts and leases reach the Board from a department after a competition the sponsor took no part in; the sponsor is often the district’s supervisor or the Mayor carrying a routine file. A supervisor sponsors files about their own district, and the businesses there are the ones most likely to have given to that supervisor, so sponsorship and giving can go together with no exchange between them. Contributions are small beside the amounts because City law caps them. Nothing here shows that any of it was connected.

tables.how: Passed Board files tied to lobbying by file number, and enacted ordinances tied by the words of the subject (marked as inferred), for clients whose contacts sought support, approval or amendment: 51 measures, 54 client rows. In 6 the measure itself names the client, for $248,670,405. Building permits are those issued within three years at the street address in the title of a zoning or development measure (10 sites, $117,432,917 of stated cost, each permit counted once although a site can sit under two files). Of 34 clients with City payments on both sides of passage, 27 were paid more after.
tables.limits: Only the amount in the measure and the permits can be read as following from it, and even those need the file: an award is usually negotiated by a department before the Board votes, and a permit at an address may belong to another owner or an earlier approval. Contracts and payments after passage are mostly unrelated work, and City spending on outside payees rose throughout these years. An amount naming the client can be money the client pays the City.

tables.how: The first version of every monthly report by a lobbyist who contacts officials (32,251 reports), with the date received set against the 15th of the month after the period: 3,039 were late (9.4%), 409 of them by more than thirty days. The deadline is the one stated in an Ethics Commission stipulation on file.
tables.limits: A late report is a filing lapse, not concealment; many are a day or two late. The file shows when a report’s first version arrived, not what it said, so an entry added later by amendment looks earlier than it was disclosed.

tables.how: A contact is listed when it names a Board file by number, is dated on or before the day of the Board’s final roll call on that file, and sits in a monthly report whose first version was late and arrived after that day: 178 contacts on 25 files. The day of the vote is read from the roll-call pages; where no final roll call is on disk, the date the file is recorded as passed is used and the row says so. The report link opens the first version of the report.
tables.limits: A late report is a filing lapse, not concealment. But a contact first disclosed after a file has passed could not be seen by anyone watching that vote. The filing file shows when the first version arrived, not what it said, so a contact added later by amendment is not caught, which makes this count a floor. Where the client is a private person (a homeowner seeking a permit, say) the client is left blank and the subject is not shown.
